extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claim additional elements amount to an "inventive concept" (i.e., whether a claim amounts to significantly more than a judicial exception) under the Alice/Mayo Step 2B analysis. Includes special considerations for treatment/prophylaxis limitations and technological/improvement-based analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment/prophylaxis must affirmatively recite an action
rubrics_metrics.description: To qualify as a “treatment” or “prophylaxis” limitation the claim limitation must affirmatively recite an action that effects a treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition (e.g., “administering amazonic acid to a patient” or “administering a course of plasmapheresis to a patient”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the limitation is merely an intended use or a field-of-use (e.g., “prescribing a topical steroid to a patient with eczema”) or merely indicates how a claimed product might be used (e.g., that a claimed product is a “pharmaceutical composition” or a dispenser “to dispense a mineral supplement”), it is not an affirmative treatment/prophylaxis limitation and cannot integrate a judicial exception under the treatment/prophylaxis consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity of treatment or prophylaxis
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatment or prophylaxis limitation must be “particular,” i.e., specifically identified so that it does not encompass all applications of the judicial exception(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: “administering a lower than normal dosage of a beta blocker medication to a patient identified as having the poor metabolizer genotype” is particular and integrates the abstract idea; by contrast, “administering a suitable medication to a patient” is generic and does not integrate the abstract idea. Examiners may evaluate related considerations such as instructions to apply an exception (MPEP § 2106.05(f)) and field of use/technological environment (MPEP § 2106.05(h)).

rubrics_metrics.name: More-than-nominal relationship to the judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatment or prophylaxis limitation must have more than a nominal or insignificant relationship to the recited judicial exception(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: treating high blood glucose (>250 mg/dl) with insulin has a significant relationship (insulin reduces glucose and the risk of ketoacidosis) and thus can integrate the law of nature into a practical application; treating the same with aspirin has at best a nominal connection and does not meaningfully apply the exception. Examiners may consult the insignificant extra-solution activity (MPEP § 2106.05(g)) and field-of-use/technological environment (MPEP § 2106.05(h)) considerations when assessing this factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not merely extra-solution activity or field-of-use
rubrics_metrics.description: A treatment or prophylaxis limitation must impose meaningful limits on the judicial exception and cannot be merely extra-solution activity (steps performed only to gather data) or mere field-of-use limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: administering vaccines solely to gather data for a mental analysis step is extra-solution activity and does not integrate the exception; but vaccinating a second group according to the lowest-risk schedule that was identified integrates the abstract idea into a practical application. Evaluate against insignificant extra-solution activity (MPEP § 2106.05(g)) and the field-of-use/technological environment consideration (MPEP § 2106.05(h)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and evaluate additional elements individually and in combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2B requires identifying additional elements (features/limitations/steps) recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception(s) and evaluating those additional elements both individually and as an ordered combination to determine whether they contribute an inventive concept (i.e., amount to significantly more).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should carry over identification of additional elements from Step 2A Prong Two and conclusions on considerations discussed in MPEP §§ 2106.05(a)-(c), (e), (f), and (h). Re-evaluate any element previously considered insignificant extra-solution activity (MPEP § 2106.05(g)) if it may be unconventional when reconsidered, and evaluate whether elements are other than well-understood, routine, conventional activities per MPEP § 2106.05(d). Claims must be considered as a whole and each claim examined separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive concept must be provided by elements beyond the judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventive concept cannot be furnished by the unpatentable law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea itself; it must be furnished by an element or combination of elements recited in the claim in addition to the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate the search for an inventive concept with novelty/non-obviousness (§§102/103) or written-description/enablement (§112) inquiries—lack of novelty or obviousness is not determinative of §101 inventive-concept analysis. Consider case law distinguishing these inquiries (e.g., Mayo, Alice, RecogniCorp).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements to functioning of a computer or other technology
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed improvement to the functioning of the computer itself or to any other technology or technical field can supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification should provide a technical explanation of how to implement the invention such that a person of ordinary skill would recognize the claimed invention as providing an improvement. The claim must reflect the disclosed improvement (the claim need not state the improvement in explicit terms but the claim scope must capture the improvement). Avoid oversimplifying claims; evaluate the claim “as a whole” as an ordered combination. Examples: DDR Holdings, Enfish, McRO, Diehr. If the specification only conclusorily asserts an improvement without detail, the examiner should not find the claim improves technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a particular machine or apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying the judicial exception with, or by use of, a particular machine (a specific machine or arrangement understood in the art) can qualify as significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: reciting a Fourdrinier machine arranged to optimize speed/quality (Eibel Process Co.). Merely naming a generic machine or generic computer components is insufficient; the arrangement/structure and how it contributes are important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effecting a transformation of a particular article to a different state or thing
rubrics_metrics.description: A process that effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing can amount to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: transforming raw uncured synthetic rubber into precision-molded synthetic rubber products (Diehr). The transformation must be meaningful and tied to the claimed steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adding specific, non-conventional limitations or unconventional arrangement of known elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding a specific limitation other than what is well-understood, routine, conventional activity in the field, or adding unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application (including a non-conventional and non-generic arrangement of known components) can supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: BASCOM — non-conventional arrangement of filtering components at a specific remote location with customizable features. The inventive concept may arise from the combination even if individual elements are known. Evaluate whether the claim recites such non-conventional arrangements or limitations (MPEP § 2106.05(d)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningful linkage to a particular technological environment may qualify
rubrics_metrics.description: Meaningfully linking the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment—for example integrating data comparison into a specific immunization process that lowers later disease risk—can be a limitation that qualifies as significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Classen Immunotherapies (immunization step integrating data comparison into a specific process). However, merely generally linking an abstract idea to a field or technological environment (e.g., use in commodities markets or limiting a formula to petrochemical field) is insufficient (see also non-qualifying list).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations that do NOT qualify as significantly more
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain types of additional elements have been found insufficient to constitute significantly more: simply appending well-understood, routine, conventional activities specified at a high level of generality; adding the words “apply it” or mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer; adding insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., mere data gathering); and generally linking the abstract idea to a technological environment or field-of-use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Alice — generic computer performing generic functions; CyberSource — mere data gathering; Bilski/Parker — general field-of-use limitation. Examiners should identify if the recited elements are no more than generic implementation or insignificant activity (MPEP §§ 2106.05(d), (f), (g), (h)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Physicality/tangibility is not by itself decisive
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere physicality or tangibility of an additional element (e.g., reciting a computer) is not a relevant consideration that by itself supplies an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A computer is a tangible machine, but reciting it does not guarantee eligibility if the claims only require generic computer functions. Conversely, the presence of a non-physical or intangible additional element does not automatically make a claim ineligible; what matters is whether the claim recites an improvement or inventive concept (see Alice, Enfish, McRO, Genetic Technologies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification support and claim-reflection of improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: If the applicant asserts that the invention improves conventional functioning, the specification must contain sufficient technical detail so a person of ordinary skill would recognize the improvement, and the claims must reflect the improvement described in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification need not state the improvement in formulaic terms, but conclusory assertions of improvement without detail are insufficient. After finding a disclosed improvement, examiners must ensure the claim itself includes components or steps that provide the improvement (claims should be considered under the broadest reasonable interpretation and evaluated as an ordered combination). Case examples: McRO (spec explained automation rules), Affinity Labs (spec failed to provide necessary detail).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B outcomes and claim-level examination
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim as a whole does not amount to significantly more than the exception (no inventive concept) then it is not eligible and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101; if the claim as a whole does amount to significantly more, it is eligible at Pathway C and the eligibility analysis is complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should examine each claim separately — claims should not be presumed to stand or fall together; a dependent claim may be eligible even if an independent claim is not. See MPEP § 2106.07 for formulating an ineligibility rejection.
